Kalendae (Calendae), Kalendārum f. pl.

noun, first declension, plural

the Kalends, the first day of the month

Named, Varro says rightly, because on that day the priests announced (calābant) the date of the Nones (LL 6.27). The month’s adjective agrees with it: Kalendae Jānuāriae, 1 January; Kalendīs Majīs, on 1 May. The days before it are counted backwards, both ends included: prīdiē Kalendās Majās is 30 April, the day before; ante diem tertium Kalendās Majās (written a. d. III Kal. Mai.) is the third day before, 29 April. Interest fell due on the Kalends, hence Horace’s trīstēs Kalendae (S. 1.3.87). For the modern way of dating, see January.

Examples

  • ante diem tertium Kalendās Majās

    on 29 April (the third day before the Kalends of May)composed

  • Kal. Majīs dē Formiānō proficīscēmur, ut Antī sīmus a. d. V Nōnās Majās

    on 1 May we shall leave Formiae, so as to be at Antium on the 3rdCic. Att. 2.8.2

  • ad Kalendās Graecās solūtūrōs

    they’ll pay on the Greek Kalends, that is, never (Augustus’ saying: the Greek calendar had no Kalends)Suet. Aug. 87.1

See also the Nones, the Ides, month, calendar, New Year’s Day.
